etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English faynt, feynt (“weak; feeble”), from Old French faint, feint (“feigned; negligent; sluggish”), past participle of feindre, faindre (“to feign; sham; work negligently”), from Latin fingere (“to touch, handle, form, shape, frame, form in thought, imagine, conceive, contrive, devise, feign”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold”). Cognate with feign and fiction and more distantly dough.

definitions.definition: (of a being) Lacking strength; weak; languid; inclined to lose consciousness
Lacking courage, spirit, or energy; cowardly; dejected

quote.text: Faint heart ne'er won fair lady.

definitions.definition: Barely perceptible; not bright, or loud, or sharp
Performed, done, or acted, weakly; not exhibiting vigor, strength, or energy

quote.citation: 2005, Plato, translated by Lesley Brown, Sophist, page 243b:
quote.text: do you have the faintest understanding of what they mean?

definitions.definition: (archaic) Sickly, so as to make a person feel faint.

quote.text: Happening to pass a fruiterer’s on their way; the door of which was open, though the shop was by this time shut; one of them remarked how faint the peaches smelled.

definitions.definition: (rare) The state of one who has fainted; a swoon.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fainten, feynten, from the adjective (see above).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To lose consciousness through a lack of oxygen or nutrients to the brain, usually as a result of suddenly reduced blood flow (may be caused by emotional trauma, loss of blood or various medical conditions).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Mark 8:8:
quote.text: If I send them away fasting  […]  they will faint by the way.

quote.citation: 1713 September 22, Richard Steele, The Guardian, number 167:
quote.text: But upon hearing the Honour which he intended her , she fainted away , and fell down as Dead at his Feet

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To lose courage or spirit; to become depressed or despondent.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 24:10:
quote.text: If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To decay; to disappear; to vanish.

quote.citation: November 12, 1711, Alexander Pope, letter to Henry Cromwell
quote.text: Gilded clouds, while we gaze upon them, faint before the eye.
